historicalContext.before: Earlier in this chapter, a man has already told his brother Simon, 'We have found the Messiah,' and Jesus has called Philip to follow him. Now Philip brings the same kind of news to his friend Nathanael. Nathanael's reply, which follows, is doubtful, since he asks whether anything good can come out of Nazareth. The chapter keeps showing people brought to Jesus by others who have already met him. Book background: John's Gospel was written so that readers may believe Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God.

historicalContext.before: The crowd has just gone out to meet Jesus with palm branches and shouts of praise, so the scene is one of welcome and excitement as he comes toward Jerusalem. Jesus then finds a young donkey and sits on it, which shapes how the arrival looks. The writer links this act to an older prophetic text, and the phrase "as it is written" is the bridge to that text. Book background: this Gospel is generally dated to around AD 90 to 100, though some date it earlier, and who wrote it is debated.

historicalContext.before: Jesus is teaching his disciples in a farewell talk, which the book background places on his last night with them before his death. Just before this, he tells them to remain in his love. Here he holds up his own obedience to the Father as the pattern they are to follow, as he prepares them for the time ahead.

theology.before: This verse shows how a person can be brought in through another person. The disciple who is known to the high priest speaks on Peter's behalf and opens the way, a small picture of how people in the Bible often draw near to God or to others through someone who goes ahead of them. Peter's place outside also reminds the reader that the story is not about Peter's own strength. In John, the central claim is that Jesus is the Son of God, and that claim is what the whole account is written to help readers believe. This verse keeps attention on who gets in and how, and on the door that stands between outside and inside.

theology.before: The verse holds together two things the Gospel keeps putting side by side. The crowd and the leaders reject Jesus as king, yet the words spoken here call him their king. John presents Jesus's kingship as real even when it is mocked or refused. The verse also places this moment on the day before Passover, the festival that looked back to God's rescue of his people, which invites the reader to see Jesus's death within that larger story. Mark 15:33 also marks the sixth hour as a time of darkness at the cross, linking the time to later events. Readers from many backgrounds have seen in this verse a stark picture of who Jesus is and how he was received.

theology.before: The verse shows the risen Jesus keeping the marks of his suffering and letting his friends see them. That fits the promise in John 16:20-22 that sorrow would turn into joy, and the wounds connect this moment with the death described in John 19:34. Luke 24:39-41 has a similar scene in which Jesus shows his hands and feet to the group. First John 1:1 speaks of what the apostles heard, saw and touched, which helps explain why seeing the risen Lord mattered so much to early believers.

theology.before: The verse shows people asking for proof before they trust, and it shows that they expect God's work to be visible and checkable. Jesus has just pointed to belief in the one God has sent as the work God asks for, so the question turns on what it means to trust him. The Bible often connects signs with faith. Exodus 4:8 describes signs given so that people might believe, while John 12:37 notes that people did not believe even after many signs. 1 Corinthians 1:22 notes that some people look for signs. John 10:38 invites people to believe because of the works. These passages show that God's acts matter, and that faith is a response of trust.

historicalContext.before: The man has already been brought before the Pharisees, and they ask him again how he got his sight. John's Gospel was written so that readers may believe Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and have life.

theology.before: In John, Jesus' healings are called signs, pointing beyond the act itself to who Jesus is. This man's witness is simple. He cannot explain everything, but he can say truthfully what happened to him. The related passages show him holding to the same account when pressed (John 9:26-27). The verse teaches that honest testimony about what we have experienced can be given even before we have all the answers.

theology.before: The verse shows that the enemy of God and people is real, and that his power has limits. Related passages describe a fall from heaven: Isaiah 14:12 uses the image of a morning star cast down, and Revelation 12:7-9 describes a war in heaven and a dragon thrown to the earth. John 12:31 speaks of the ruler of this world being cast out, and Hebrews 2:14 says Jesus shared in humanity so that through death he might destroy the one who holds the power of death. Christians read these passages in different ways. Some see the fall as happening before creation, and others link it to Jesus's death and victory. The verse itself does not settle when it happened.

historicalContext.before: The verse sits in a passage where a crowd is present and where the warnings look ahead to people who will oppose those being addressed. Just before it, the words tell the hearers not to fear people who can only kill the body, and they promise that God knows even the hairs of their heads. Verse 11 then speaks of being brought before synagogues, rulers and authorities. Luke's Gospel uses a long journey to Jerusalem as one of its main settings, and this teaching belongs to that wider flow of the story.

lifeInBibleTimes.before: Synagogues were local meeting places where people gathered, especially on the Sabbath, and they were often the setting for community matters. Verse 11 mentions being brought before synagogues, rulers and authorities, which suggests the pressure in view came from public settings and local authority figures, not only from private arguments. Knowing this helps explain why the verse talks about denying someone 'in the presence of men', since being known publicly was part of everyday life in such communities.

theology.before: The verse shows that God's invitation is real and that people can turn it down. The first guests had been called, and they did not come, so the table was opened to others. Other parts of the Bible use similar pictures. Matthew 22:8 tells a related story of a wedding feast where the invited guests were not ready. Acts 13:46 shows the message going to outsiders after some listeners rejected it. John 3:19 speaks of light and darkness, and John 3:36 of belief in the Son as the dividing line. The word 'chosen' is read differently: some Christians link it to God's own choosing before time, others to a person's response to the call. The verse itself does not settle that debate.

didYouKnow.before: In the Greek, the word for 'this' comes right after the word for 'age', so the phrase reads 'the sons of this age'. That pairing is why the phrase points to the present time of life.
didYouKnow.after: The Greek phrase behind 'the children of this world' uses huioi, 'sons', and aiōnos, 'age', so it reads 'the sons of this age'. The word aiōnos points to a stretch of time, which is why the phrase speaks of people living in the present age.

lifeInBibleTimes.before: Synagogues were local gathering places where people met, especially on the Sabbath, to hear Scripture read and explained. Luke 4:15 says he taught in their synagogues, and the passage after shows him standing up to read from a scroll of Isaiah. Scrolls were rolled and unrolled as the reader found a place, and a reader often stood to read aloud. Scholars do not agree on every detail of synagogue worship in this period, but the basic picture of a local meeting for reading and teaching is well established.

historicalContext.before: This moment comes right after Jesus meets a funeral procession at the gate of Nain, a town mentioned in the verses given. The Gospel of Luke pays close attention to the poor and to women, which helps explain why this widow's story is told in such detail.

theology.before: The verse shows that a person's real life is worth more than anything the world can offer, and that gaining the world cannot buy back a lost self. Psalm 49:6-8 says that wealth cannot ransom a life, which gives a similar message from the Old Testament. Matthew 16:26 and Mark 8:36 record a parallel saying, so the teaching is not confined to one place. Luke 12:19-21 tells of a rich man who piles up goods for himself and then dies, and Luke 4:5-7 shows the devil offering all the kingdoms of the world. Both show how strongly the world's wealth can pull at a heart. The verse points to God as the one who gives a life its true worth.

didYouKnow.before: Look at where the small word for not sits in the Greek. It comes directly before the verb 'they did receive', so the refusal is stated right at the start of the sentence.
didYouKnow.after: The Greek word prosōpon means 'face', and it is the word used here for the face of Jesus. The verse says his face was set toward Jerusalem, a plain way of saying he was heading there, and that direction is the reason given for why the village would not receive him.

theology.before: The verse shows that God cares about the inner life, the heart, and not only outward actions. The speaker commits to keeping away from what is crooked in both heart and deed, which reflects the idea that faith shapes what we allow near us. Proverbs 11:20 says that those with a perverse heart are an abomination to the LORD, so God's view of a twisted heart is firm. The call not to be yoked unequally with unbelievers in 2 Corinthians 6:14-16, and the charge to depart from iniquity in 2 Timothy 2:19, carry a similar concern for separating from what is wrong. The verse presents this as a sincere personal commitment, not a claim to already be perfect.

historicalContext.before: The heading attributes this psalm to David, though the book background notes that headings are disputed. The psalm has moved from a call to praise into a list of what the LORD does and who he is. It has just named him merciful, gracious, slow to anger and abundant in loving kindness. This line draws the conclusion for how he deals with his people over time. Its wording continues by saying he has not treated us as our sins deserve, so the verse is presented as a reason for thankfulness rather than a warning.

theology.before: The verse shows God as the one who makes plants grow and so provides food for animals and people. Human work is part of the picture, since people cultivate the ground, yet the growth itself is God's gift. Genesis 1:11-12 describes plants producing seed and fruit at God's word, while Genesis 3:18 connects the ground with hard labor after the first humans turned away from God. Psalm 145:15-16 pictures all living things looking to God for food in its season, and Psalm 147:8-9 says he makes grass grow on the mountains. First Corinthians 3:7 echoes this: the planter and the waterer count for little, because God gives the growth. The verse invites trust in God as the source of daily bread.

theology.before: This verse shows God as the one who has power over the sea and its wildest moods. The people in the psalm cannot control the storm, but God can turn it to calm. The same picture appears in the Gospels, where Jesus calms a storm on the lake and the people in the boat are amazed, as in Matthew 8:26, Mark 4:39-41 and Luke 8:23-25. Psalm 65:7 and Psalm 89:9 also speak of God quieting the roaring seas, and Jonah 1:15 shows the sea growing calm after Jonah is thrown in. Together these passages suggest that God's power over the chaos of nature is part of who he is, and that people can bring their fear to him.

historicalContext.before: The psalm moves from a plea for help in verse 6 to a word of confidence here. The lines that follow claim more territory and name Moab, Edom and Philistia, and then the psalm asks for help against the enemy and ends by trusting that God will tread down our enemies. Shechem and Succoth are place names in the land of Israel, and the verse names them without explaining them. The book of Psalms is a collection of many poems, and the heading attributes this psalm to David, though whether headings are original is disputed.

theology.before: The verse shows a person who feels small and looked down on but keeps God's instructions in view. That connects to Psalm 22:6, where the psalmist also describes being scorned, and to Psalm 40:17, where the poor and needy are held in God's thoughts. Psalm 119:109 says the speaker keeps God's law close even in danger, and Proverbs 3:1 urges the reader not to forget teaching. In the New Testament, Luke 6:20 calls the poor blessed, James 2:5 says God chose the poor in the world to be rich in faith, and 2 Corinthians 8:9 says Jesus, though rich, became poor for others. Together these passages suggest God is especially near to those the world overlooks.

theology.before: The verse shows that God's people can feel the weight of living among those who reject peace, and it is honest about that weight rather than hiding it. It treats the soul as something that can be worn down by a long stay in a hostile setting. The wider Bible speaks to the same tension. Matthew 10:16 pictures followers sent out among hostile people, asked to be wise and harmless at once. Matthew 10:36 says a person's enemies may come from their own household. theology.before: This verse shows God as the one whose Name and Word stand above everything. theology.before: This verse shows an honest person before God. The psalmist does not pretend he has a clever answer or a strong defense. He admits he has gone quiet. Fear here means reverent honor rather than terror. The wider Bible links this hope to a ruler whose reign God establishes for a long time. Psalm 89:36-37 uses similar sun and moon imagery for David's line. Daniel 7:14 speaks of a figure given everlasting dominion that all peoples serve, and Revelation 11:15 says the kingdoms of the world become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. Jewish and Christian readers differ on how this psalm's king relates to these later hopes, and this verse alone does not settle that question.

didYouKnow.before: Look at the word that follows islands. The ordinary Hebrew word for many comes after the noun it describes, so the phrase reads roughly islands, many. That word order is how the multitude of islands is expressed in this line.
didYouKnow.after: Look at the word ravim, 'many', which follows iyim, 'islands'. The ordinary Hebrew word for many comes after the noun it describes, so the phrase reads roughly islands, many. That word order is how the multitude of islands is expressed in this line.
